groups.title: Values and references
groups.mechanism: Java always passes arguments by value; for objects the copied value is a reference. Reassigning a parameter changes the local copy, while mutating its referent can affect the caller.
groups.tradeOff: Sharing reduces copying but requires an ownership and mutation contract.
groups.verify: Pass one mutable object to two callers; distinguish reassignment, mutation and defensive copying.

questions.question: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.answer: Always pass-by-value. An object argument copies a reference value, allowing shared-object mutation without allowing the callee to replace the caller's variable.

questions.question: When should an API defensively copy a collection?
questions.answer: Copy when retaining a caller-owned mutable collection would violate the receiving object's invariants. Decide separately whether mutable elements also need copying.

questions.question: Why does reassigning an object parameter not replace the caller's object?
questions.answer: The parameter is a separate variable initialized with the reference value. Assignment changes that variable rather than the caller's variable.

questions.question: How can an immutable-looking object still change unexpectedly?
questions.answer: A final reference can point to mutable state. Constructor inputs and accessor results can expose that state unless copied or confined.

questions.question: How would you define ownership for a high-throughput message object?
questions.answer: Specify who may mutate it and when ownership transfers. Choose immutable data or confinement, then measure copying costs before sharing mutable buffers.

groups.title: Equality and hashing
groups.mechanism: Hash collections locate candidate buckets using hashes and distinguish keys with equality. Equal objects must share a hash; unequal objects may collide.
groups.tradeOff: Value equality simplifies lookup but requires stable equality-relevant state while keys are stored.
groups.verify: Test equal distinct instances, collisions, null handling and mutation after insertion.

questions.question: How do identity and equality differ?
questions.answer: Identity asks whether references designate the same object. Equality can express equivalent values according to the type's equals contract.

questions.question: When must equals and hashCode be implemented together?
questions.answer: Whenever value equality is customized for use in hash-based collections. Equal instances must produce equal hash codes.

questions.question: Why can a changed map key become unreachable?
questions.answer: Changing fields used by hashCode or equals invalidates the lookup assumptions associated with the key's original insertion.

questions.question: Does the same hash code imply two objects are equal?
questions.answer: No. Collisions are permitted; the collection still uses equality to identify the matching key.

questions.question: How would you review equality across a class hierarchy?
questions.answer: Check symmetry, transitivity and substitutability. Prefer explicit value semantics or composition where subclass state would make inherited equality inconsistent.

groups.title: Collections and ordering
groups.mechanism: List, Set and Map encode different identity, duplication and ordering contracts. Choose implementations from access patterns rather than interchangeable syntax.
groups.tradeOff: An ordering guarantee often carries memory or update costs.
groups.verify: Exercise duplicates, empty input, iteration order and concurrent modification under the promised contract.

questions.question: How do List, Set and Map differ?
questions.answer: Lists represent sequences, sets represent uniqueness, and maps associate keys with values. Each implementation adds its own ordering and concurrency guarantees.

questions.question: When is ArrayList preferable to LinkedList?
questions.answer: Usually for indexed access and iteration because of compact storage and locality. LinkedList insertion still requires locating the node through its public API.

questions.question: What does a comparator need to guarantee?
questions.answer: A consistent ordering relation. In sorted sets, comparison returning zero determines uniqueness, which can differ from equals if designed inconsistently.

questions.question: Why is fail-fast iteration not a concurrency guarantee?
questions.answer: ConcurrentModificationException is a best-effort bug detector. It does not make unsynchronized concurrent access correct or reliably detect every race.

questions.question: How do you preserve deterministic output from a map-based aggregation?
questions.answer: Select an ordered representation or explicitly sort the result using a stable total order. Do not depend on incidental hash iteration order.

groups.title: HashMap internals
groups.mechanism: HashMap uses bucket indexing, equality-based collision resolution and resizing. Tree bins improve sufficiently crowded buckets under implementation-specific thresholds.
groups.tradeOff: Expected constant-time access depends on hashing, resizing and workload; it is not a universal worst-case guarantee.
groups.verify: Measure collision-heavy keys, resize pressure and key stability with representative cardinality.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a HashMap load factor?
questions.answer: It controls the occupancy threshold that triggers resizing. Higher occupancy can save space while increasing collision-related work.

questions.question: Why pre-size a frequently populated map?
questions.answer: An appropriate initial capacity can reduce repeated growth and rehashing. Over-sizing also wastes memory, so derive it from expected entries.

questions.question: How does HashMap distinguish keys sharing a bucket?
questions.answer: It compares candidate key hashes and equality, using linked or tree structures depending on implementation state.

questions.question: What happens if several threads mutate a HashMap without coordination?
questions.answer: There is no thread-safety guarantee. Updates and reads can race, lose information or observe inconsistent state.

questions.question: How would you choose between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap?
questions.answer: Use HashMap for confined or externally synchronized state. Use ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent operations, while separately protecting multi-key business invariants.

groups.title: Generics and variance
groups.mechanism: Java generics provide compile-time type checking, largely through erasure. Invariance prevents unsafe writes; wildcards express restricted reading or writing capabilities.
groups.tradeOff: Flexible signatures can become harder to understand if wildcards spread through internal code.
groups.verify: Compile representative subtype calls and deliberately unsafe writes; inspect raw-type warnings.

questions.question: Why is List<Integer> not a subtype of List<Number>?
questions.answer: If it were, a caller could add a Double through the Number view and violate the Integer list's element contract.

questions.question: What does producer-extends consumer-super mean?
questions.answer: Read values through extends bounds and accept writes through super bounds. Choose variance from the operation's permitted use, not a memorized annotation pattern.

questions.question: What information does erasure remove at runtime?
questions.answer: Most generic type arguments are not reified on instances. Runtime checks cannot generally distinguish List<String> from List<Integer>.

questions.question: Why can raw types produce a delayed ClassCastException?
questions.answer: Raw access bypasses generic checks and permits incompatible values. The failure may appear later when a typed read inserts a cast.

questions.question: How can an API preserve useful generic type information for serialization?
questions.answer: Use an explicit type token or framework-supported generic descriptor. A raw Class<List> does not capture the desired element type.

groups.title: Exceptions and cleanup
groups.mechanism: Exceptions represent abrupt completion; resource ownership must still be resolved. Try-with-resources closes declared resources and preserves secondary close failures as suppressed exceptions.
groups.tradeOff: Checked exceptions expose handling obligations but can complicate APIs when the recovery contract is unclear.
groups.verify: Fail both the body and close operation; inspect the primary and suppressed failures.

questions.question: How do checked and unchecked exceptions differ?
questions.answer: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared under language rules. Unchecked exceptions do not require that declaration, but still need an intentional error policy.

questions.question: When should an exception be translated at a boundary?
questions.answer: When a lower-level failure needs a stable domain or API meaning. Preserve the cause and avoid exposing secret-bearing internal messages.

questions.question: What is a suppressed exception in try-with-resources?
questions.answer: A secondary failure, commonly during close, attached to the primary failure so cleanup does not hide the original problem.

questions.question: Why is returning from finally dangerous?
questions.answer: It can replace a return value or suppress an exception from the try block, obscuring the actual outcome.

questions.question: How should interruption be handled in reusable library code?
questions.answer: Propagate InterruptedException when possible, or restore the interrupt flag when translating it. Do not silently consume cancellation signals.

groups.title: Immutability and records
groups.mechanism: Records define transparent data carriers with generated component-based methods. Their final component references do not recursively freeze referenced objects.
groups.tradeOff: Immutability simplifies sharing but may require copying and deliberate representation choices.
groups.verify: Mutate supplied collections after construction and verify the record's promised value stability.

questions.question: What does a Java record provide?
questions.answer: A component declaration with generated accessors, constructor-related behavior and value-oriented equals, hashCode and toString implementations.

questions.question: When is a normal class better than a record?
questions.answer: When identity, controlled mutable state, inheritance requirements or hidden representation are central to the type's contract.

questions.question: How can a compact record constructor validate inputs?
questions.answer: Validate constructor parameters and normalize or defensively copy mutable inputs before the implicit component assignment occurs.

questions.question: Why is a record containing an array not deeply immutable?
questions.answer: The array remains mutable, and generated equality uses the component's equality semantics rather than automatically providing deep array equality.

questions.question: How would you evolve a public record without breaking consumers?
questions.answer: Treat component additions and changes as constructor, serialization and behavioral contract changes. Introduce versioned DTOs or explicit compatibility boundaries.

groups.title: Streams and collectors
groups.mechanism: Streams describe a pipeline over a source; terminal operations drive traversal. Intermediate operations should avoid interfering with the source or depending on incidental execution order.
groups.tradeOff: Declarative pipelines improve composition but can conceal allocation, ordering and repeated work.
groups.verify: Test empty input, duplicates, ordering, null policies and a sequential reference result.

questions.question: What makes a stream operation lazy?
questions.answer: Intermediate operations generally describe work that is executed when a terminal operation consumes the pipeline.

questions.question: When should map be replaced by flatMap?
questions.answer: Use flatMap when each input produces zero or more elements and the desired output is one flattened stream.

questions.question: What is required of a parallel reduction operation?
questions.answer: Its combining operation must be associative with a valid identity; mutable accumulation also needs a correct collector contract.

questions.question: Why can peek-based side effects disappear or behave unexpectedly?
questions.answer: Stream optimizations and traversal requirements can alter which elements are evaluated. Use explicit terminal logic for required effects.

questions.question: How would you evaluate replacing a loop with a parallel stream?
questions.answer: Measure task size, splitting cost, ordering, shared state and pool contention. Blocking downstream work needs its own bounded execution strategy.

groups.title: Optional and null contracts
groups.mechanism: Optional models expected absence at a return boundary. It does not describe why infrastructure failed or authorize arbitrary use of null.
groups.tradeOff: Explicit absence improves callers' decisions but wrappers can complicate persistence and serialization models.
groups.verify: Test absent, present and exceptional results without using unchecked get calls.

questions.question: What problem does Optional solve?
questions.answer: It makes expected absence visible in a return type and encourages callers to choose an explicit alternative path.

questions.question: How do orElse and orElseGet differ?
questions.answer: orElse evaluates its argument before the call. orElseGet invokes its supplier only when the Optional is empty.

questions.question: What is the difference between map and flatMap on Optional?
questions.answer: map wraps a mapping result when present; flatMap accepts an Optional-producing function and avoids nested Optional values.

questions.question: Why should a database outage not become Optional.empty?
questions.answer: It would confuse a failed lookup with a successful lookup that found no record, potentially causing destructive business decisions.

questions.question: How would you design an API with missing, forbidden and failed outcomes?
questions.answer: Represent these outcomes explicitly through domain results or documented exceptions; do not collapse them into one null or empty value.

groups.title: Java memory model
groups.mechanism: Happens-before relationships establish visibility and ordering between actions. Data-race freedom requires appropriate synchronization or ownership, not merely lucky observation.
groups.tradeOff: Coordination provides correctness but may add contention; confinement can remove sharing altogether.
groups.verify: Exercise real concurrent access and verify invariants rather than using sleep to assume timing.

questions.question: What does volatile guarantee?
questions.answer: Visibility and ordering associated with reads and writes of that variable. It does not make a compound operation such as increment atomic.

questions.question: When does synchronized provide visibility?
questions.answer: Unlocking a monitor happens-before a later successful lock of that same monitor, alongside mutual exclusion for the protected region.

questions.question: What is safe publication?
questions.answer: Making an object's initialized state visible to other threads through a supported happens-before mechanism such as synchronization or concurrent containers.

questions.question: Why can double-checked locking fail without volatile?
questions.answer: The publication path can expose a reference without the required initialization visibility guarantees. Correct Java implementations use volatile for that pattern.

questions.question: How would you reduce contention without weakening correctness?
questions.answer: Identify the protected invariant first, then consider confinement, immutable snapshots, partitioning or narrower synchronization with measured contention evidence.

groups.title: Locks and atomics
groups.mechanism: Atomic classes support specific indivisible updates; locks protect larger state transitions. Neither automatically defines the business invariant being preserved.
groups.tradeOff: Lock-free updates can reduce blocking but retries and multi-variable coordination still have costs.
groups.verify: Test conflicting updates and cancellation while checking the full invariant.

questions.question: When is AtomicInteger preferable to volatile int?
questions.answer: When the operation needs atomic read-modify-write behavior such as increment, compare-and-set or update functions.

questions.question: Why can two atomic variables still produce an inconsistent pair?
questions.answer: Each variable is updated atomically, but the relationship between both updates is not atomic unless explicitly coordinated.

questions.question: What does compare-and-set establish?
questions.answer: An update succeeds only if the currently observed value matches the expected value under the primitive's comparison semantics.

questions.question: What is the ABA problem?
questions.answer: A value changes from A to B and back to A, hiding intermediate history from a comparison that checks only the current value.

questions.question: How would you choose between a lock and a CAS retry loop?
questions.answer: Compare invariant size, contention, retry cost, fairness and cancellation requirements. Prefer a clear correct lock over a fragile pseudo-lock-free design.

groups.title: Executors and overload
groups.mechanism: An executor separates submission from execution. Queueing, worker capacity and rejection policy together determine overload behavior and retained memory.
groups.tradeOff: Queues smooth short bursts but unbounded queues convert overload into delay and memory growth.
groups.verify: Saturate workers, exceed queue capacity and verify rejection plus graceful shutdown.

questions.question: What is the difference between execute and submit?
questions.answer: execute accepts a task without a result Future. submit returns a Future whose failure must be observed to avoid silent task errors.

questions.question: Why must an executor queue be bounded deliberately?
questions.answer: Queued work retains inputs and consumes request deadlines. An unbounded backlog can exhaust memory while throughput remains unchanged.

questions.question: How do shutdown and shutdownNow differ?
questions.answer: shutdown rejects new tasks and allows accepted work to finish. shutdownNow attempts interruption and returns tasks that never started; termination remains cooperative.

questions.question: Why can CallerRunsPolicy harm a request thread?
questions.answer: It executes rejected work on the submitting thread, potentially moving blocking or expensive work onto an event loop or latency-sensitive caller.

questions.question: How would you size concurrency for a database-backed workload?
questions.answer: Start with downstream capacity and service time, then measure throughput and queueing. More workers cannot create extra database capacity.

groups.title: Futures and cancellation
groups.mechanism: CompletableFuture composes completions; execution and cancellation depend on how work is launched and implemented. Timing out a dependent result does not undo remote effects.
groups.tradeOff: Composition simplifies asynchronous dependencies but can obscure ownership and exception propagation.
groups.verify: Complete sources exceptionally, cancel one dependent and verify sibling behavior and actual resource cleanup.

questions.question: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose?
questions.answer: thenApply transforms a completed value; thenCompose flattens a function returning another CompletionStage into one composed stage.

questions.question: When is handle preferable to exceptionally?
questions.answer: Use handle when both success and failure must produce a transformed result. exceptionally handles only exceptional completion.

questions.question: Does allOf return a list of component results?
questions.answer: No. It returns a completion stage indicating aggregate completion; obtain individual results separately under an explicit failure policy.

questions.question: Does cancelling a CompletableFuture necessarily interrupt its underlying work?
questions.answer: No. CompletableFuture cancellation does not generally control the execution mechanism; cancellation of the actual task or operation needs separate ownership.

questions.question: How would you enforce an end-to-end asynchronous deadline?
questions.answer: Allocate budget across acquisition and I/O, propagate remaining time, stop useful work cooperatively and reconcile effects whose remote outcome is unknown.

groups.title: Virtual threads
groups.mechanism: Java 21 virtual threads multiplex onto carrier threads and can unmount during supported blocking operations. They improve waiting concurrency, not CPU speed or connection capacity.
groups.tradeOff: Cheaper waiting permits more outstanding work, which can overwhelm finite dependencies without admission limits.
groups.verify: Measure retained requests, connection waits and Java 21 pinning under representative load.

questions.question: What workload benefits from virtual threads?
questions.answer: Many concurrent tasks spending substantial time waiting for blocking I/O, provided downstream resources and admission are controlled.

questions.question: Should virtual threads be pooled like platform workers?
questions.answer: Normally create one per task rather than pooling them to limit resources. Use explicit limits around the scarce dependency itself.

questions.question: How does Java 21 monitor pinning affect virtual threads?
questions.answer: Blocking while holding certain synchronized monitors can pin a carrier in Java 21. Later JDK behavior differs, so verify the deployed runtime.

questions.question: Why can virtual threads make database latency worse?
questions.answer: They can admit many more waiting requests against the same finite pool, increasing queue time without increasing database throughput.

questions.question: How would you migrate a thread-local-heavy service to virtual threads?
questions.answer: Audit per-thread resource cost, context lifetime and cleanup. Avoid treating each virtual thread as a place to cache expensive reusable clients.

groups.title: Garbage collection
groups.mechanism: Garbage collection reclaims unreachable managed objects. Reachability, allocation rate and retained live data determine pressure; a collector cannot free strongly reachable leaked state.
groups.tradeOff: Lower pauses, throughput and footprint compete; collector selection requires workload evidence.
groups.verify: Correlate allocation, post-GC live set, pause distributions and application latency during a controlled soak.

questions.question: What is a garbage-collection root?
questions.answer: A starting point for reachability analysis, such as live thread references and certain runtime-held references, from which retained objects are traced.

questions.question: How do allocation pressure and a retention leak differ?
questions.answer: Allocation pressure creates many short-lived objects; a retention leak keeps unneeded objects reachable so the live set grows over time.

questions.question: Why does System.gc not provide a cleanup contract?
questions.answer: It is a request to the runtime, not a guarantee of immediate collection or resource release. Close owned resources explicitly.

questions.question: Why can increasing heap size worsen an incident?
questions.answer: It can postpone exhaustion while increasing memory cost or changing pause behavior, without fixing unbounded retention or downstream bottlenecks.

questions.question: How would you choose a garbage collector for a service?
questions.answer: Use supported collectors and compare throughput, tail pauses, memory headroom and operational tooling under the real container limits.

groups.title: Class loading and initialization
groups.mechanism: Class identity includes its defining class loader. Loading, linking and initialization are distinct phases with different failure modes.
groups.tradeOff: Custom loading enables isolation but complicates compatibility, unloading and diagnostics.
groups.verify: Test missing dependencies, initialization failures and repeated deployment with retained loader references.

questions.question: What is the difference between loading and initialization?
questions.answer: Loading obtains a class representation; initialization executes class initialization logic when required by language and runtime rules.

questions.question: Why can two identical class names fail a cast?
questions.answer: If defined by different class loaders, they can represent distinct runtime types despite having the same binary name.

questions.question: What can cause NoClassDefFoundError after a class previously existed?
questions.answer: A required definition may be unavailable, or initialization may have failed earlier. Inspect the original failure and loader path.

questions.question: How can an application retain an obsolete class loader?
questions.answer: Long-lived threads, static registries, callbacks or thread-local values can retain classes and their defining loader after redeployment.

questions.question: How would you diagnose a dependency linkage failure?
questions.answer: Identify the actual loaded artifact and class loader, inspect resolved dependencies and binary signatures, then correct the owning dependency conflict.

groups.title: I/O and buffers
groups.mechanism: I/O APIs differ in buffering, blocking and ownership. Character encoding and byte boundaries must be explicit; a buffer's position and limit define the active region.
groups.tradeOff: Buffer reuse reduces allocation but introduces lifecycle and aliasing risks.
groups.verify: Test partial reads, multibyte text, truncated input and resource closure on failure.

questions.question: How do byte streams and character readers differ?
questions.answer: Byte streams process raw bytes; readers decode characters using a charset. Choose an explicit charset for external data.

questions.question: Why must code handle a partial read?
questions.answer: A read may return fewer bytes than requested without reaching end-of-stream. Continue according to the protocol's framing rules.

questions.question: What does ByteBuffer.flip do?
questions.answer: It sets the limit to the current position and resets position to zero, preparing the region just written for reading.

questions.question: Why can sharing a reusable buffer corrupt asynchronous results?
questions.answer: A producer can overwrite bytes before a consumer finishes. Transfer ownership, copy the required region or use controlled reference management.

questions.question: How would you design a bounded file-upload pipeline?
questions.answer: Limit total bytes, buffered chunks and concurrent uploads; stream to owned storage and ensure cancellation removes incomplete artifacts safely.

groups.title: Time and numerical correctness
groups.mechanism: Instant represents a point on the timeline; local date-time needs zone rules for interpretation. Exact decimal arithmetic still requires explicit scale and rounding policy.
groups.tradeOff: Precision, representation and business interpretation must be selected together.
groups.verify: Test overflow, DST boundaries, negative amounts and rounding at policy boundaries.

questions.question: When should Instant be preferred to LocalDateTime?
questions.answer: For an unambiguous timestamp representing an event on the timeline. Use local date-time for a wall-clock value with explicit zone interpretation.

questions.question: Why should BigDecimal usually be constructed from decimal text?
questions.answer: A double may already contain binary floating-point approximation. Text preserves the intended decimal representation before arithmetic and rounding.

questions.question: How do BigDecimal equals and compareTo differ?
questions.answer: equals includes scale in equality; compareTo compares numerical ordering, so numerically equal values with different scales can compare as zero.

questions.question: Why can adding 24 hours differ from adding a calendar day?
questions.answer: Daylight-saving transitions can change the elapsed duration between local times on adjacent calendar dates.

questions.question: How would you keep time-dependent tests deterministic?
questions.answer: Inject a Clock or equivalent time source, control zones explicitly, and test policy boundaries without sleeping on wall-clock time.

groups.title: Diagnostics and performance
groups.mechanism: Performance conclusions require separating CPU, waiting, allocation and contention. A profile is a sample of a workload, not proof that every hot frame should be rewritten.
groups.tradeOff: Diagnostics themselves have cost and may expose sensitive data.
groups.verify: Reproduce the workload, capture before-and-after evidence and confirm the optimization preserves behavior.

questions.question: What does a CPU profile show?
questions.answer: Where executing threads spend sampled CPU time. It does not directly account for every blocked request's elapsed waiting time.

questions.question: When is a thread dump useful?
questions.answer: For blocked threads, lock contention, deadlocks and repeated execution patterns. Correlate multiple snapshots with workload and latency evidence.

questions.question: What can a heap dominator tree reveal?
questions.answer: Objects responsible for retaining substantial reachable memory and paths through which removing one owner could release retained objects.

questions.question: Why are ad hoc microbenchmarks often misleading?
questions.answer: JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination, constant folding and measurement overhead can dominate. Use an appropriate harness and representative inputs.

questions.question: How would you prove a performance change is production-worthy?
questions.answer: Demonstrate correct outputs, improved relevant latency or cost, bounded memory and stable behavior under sustained representative load and failure conditions.

groups.title: API compatibility and testing
groups.mechanism: Compatibility includes source, binary, wire and behavioral contracts. A change that compiles locally can still break older callers or persisted data.
groups.tradeOff: A smaller surface is easier to evolve, but explicit migration may be needed for meaningful changes.
groups.verify: Run boundary tests with old inputs and representative consumers; inspect actual public signatures.

questions.question: How do source and binary compatibility differ?
questions.answer: Source compatibility concerns recompilation; binary compatibility concerns existing compiled callers linking against the changed library without recompilation.

questions.question: When is an unchecked exception a compatibility concern?
questions.answer: When callers rely on documented successful behavior, failure type or recovery paths. Checked signatures are not the whole behavioral contract.

questions.question: Why can changing a collection's ordering break an API?
questions.answer: Consumers may depend on documented or historically promised order for pagination, output stability or business precedence.

questions.question: What makes a regression test meaningful?
questions.answer: It exercises an observable invariant or failure path and would fail when the defect returns, rather than repeating internal implementation details.

questions.question: How would you release an incompatible public API improvement?
questions.answer: Provide explicit versioning or deprecation, preserve old behavior during transition, test real consumer cases and document migration plus rollback constraints.

groups.title: Primitives and numeric promotion
groups.mechanism: Primitive operations follow language conversion and overflow rules. Wider assignment does not undo overflow that already occurred in a narrower expression.
groups.tradeOff: Compact primitive storage needs explicit range and precision policy.
groups.verify: Test minimum, maximum, negative and mixed-type arithmetic inputs.

questions.question: How do primitives differ from wrapper objects?
questions.answer: Primitives represent built-in values; wrappers are reference types that support generics and null but introduce boxing and identity considerations.

questions.question: When can unboxing throw NullPointerException?
questions.answer: When a null wrapper is converted to its primitive value, including implicit arithmetic or comparison contexts.

questions.question: Why can assigning an int multiplication to long still overflow?
questions.answer: The multiplication may execute as int before assignment. Promote an operand or use an exact checked operation before the calculation.

questions.question: Why should wrapper values not be compared with == for value equality?
questions.answer: Identity caching can make some comparisons appear correct while others fail. Use value equality with an explicit null policy.

questions.question: How would you protect a numeric business invariant?
questions.answer: Define valid ranges and rounding, use checked arithmetic where needed and test overflow rather than assuming larger sample inputs remain representative.

groups.title: Strings and Unicode
groups.mechanism: String stores text with UTF-16 indexing semantics; code units, code points and user-perceived characters differ. Charset conversion applies at byte boundaries.
groups.tradeOff: Simple indexing is efficient but can split supplementary characters or grapheme sequences.
groups.verify: Test supplementary characters, combining marks and malformed external encodings.

questions.question: Why is String immutable?
questions.answer: Its public contract does not permit changing an existing string's value, supporting safe sharing and stable string-key behavior.

questions.question: When should StringBuilder be used?
questions.answer: For repeated local string construction where mutable accumulation improves clarity or avoids excessive intermediate strings; measure meaningful hot paths.

questions.question: How does intern differ from ordinary string equality?
questions.answer: Interning obtains a canonical string reference for a value; equals compares values regardless of whether the instances share identity.

questions.question: Why can char-based truncation corrupt visible text?
questions.answer: A char is a UTF-16 code unit, so truncation can split surrogate pairs or user-perceived character sequences.

questions.question: How would you process external text safely?
questions.answer: Choose an explicit charset, bound input size, handle invalid sequences intentionally and distinguish protocol identifiers from locale-sensitive display text.

groups.title: Object-oriented dispatch
groups.mechanism: Overloading selects a signature from compile-time information; overriding supplies runtime behavior for eligible virtual calls. Constructors and static methods have different rules.
groups.tradeOff: Inheritance offers substitution while composition often reduces lifecycle and equality coupling.
groups.verify: Exercise calls through base references, null arguments and overloaded signatures.

questions.question: How do overloading and overriding differ?
questions.answer: Overloading provides different parameter signatures; overriding supplies subtype behavior for an inherited eligible instance method.

questions.question: When is composition preferable to inheritance?
questions.answer: When reuse does not require a true substitutable subtype and independent responsibilities or lifecycle would otherwise become tightly coupled.

questions.question: How does runtime method dispatch choose an override?
questions.answer: For eligible virtual invocation, the actual receiver type determines the overriding implementation after the call's signature is selected.

questions.question: Why can overloading with unrelated reference types make null ambiguous?
questions.answer: The compiler may find no uniquely most-specific applicable overload for a null argument.

questions.question: How would you review a subclass for substitutability?
questions.answer: Check accepted inputs, promised outcomes, exceptions and state invariants so callers relying on the base contract remain correct.

groups.title: Access and initialization order
groups.mechanism: Accessibility, static initialization and instance construction follow separate language rules. Calling overridable methods from constructors can expose incompletely initialized subclass state.
groups.tradeOff: Convenience initialization can create hidden ordering and startup dependencies.
groups.verify: Construct subclasses with overridden methods and test initialization failure paths.

questions.question: How do public, protected and package-private access differ?
questions.answer: They define different visibility boundaries across classes, packages and subclasses; use the narrowest access that serves the intended API.

questions.question: When should static state be avoided?
questions.answer: When mutable global ownership would couple tests, users or class-loader lifetimes and make initialization or cleanup difficult.

questions.question: How is static initialization different from an instance constructor?
questions.answer: Static initialization establishes class-level state when required; each constructor participates in creating one object and its instance state.

questions.question: Why is calling an overridable method from a constructor risky?
questions.answer: The override can run before subclass fields are initialized, observing invalid default values or escaping the partially constructed object.

questions.question: How would you remove fragile initialization ordering?
questions.answer: Make required state explicit through construction, avoid hidden global callbacks and separate bounded startup coordination from object constructors.

groups.title: Enums and sealed hierarchies
groups.mechanism: Enums represent a fixed named set of instances; sealed hierarchies constrain permitted subtypes. Both help model closed alternatives without using arbitrary strings.
groups.tradeOff: Closed models improve exhaustiveness but additions can affect persistence and consumer compatibility.
groups.verify: Add a new alternative and inspect switches, serialized values and older readers.

questions.question: When is an enum preferable to string constants?
questions.answer: When the domain has a controlled set of alternatives and type checking should prevent arbitrary invalid values.

questions.question: What does a sealed class constrain?
questions.answer: Which types may directly extend or implement it under Java's permitted-subtype rules.

questions.question: How can pattern matching simplify a closed hierarchy?
questions.answer: It combines type testing and binding, and supported switch forms can help express exhaustive handling of known alternatives.

questions.question: Why is persisting enum ordinal dangerous?
questions.answer: Reordering or inserting constants changes ordinal meanings and can reinterpret historical data without an obvious schema change.

questions.question: How would you evolve a closed state model?
questions.answer: Use stable persisted codes, explicit transitions and tolerant migration boundaries; test old data and readers before adding or removing alternatives.

groups.title: Annotations and retention
groups.mechanism: Annotations provide metadata consumed by compilers, processors or runtime frameworks. Retention controls availability; an annotation has no intrinsic business effect without a consumer.
groups.tradeOff: Metadata reduces boilerplate while making processing and invocation paths part of correctness.
groups.verify: Compile with and without the processor and inspect runtime metadata under each retention policy.

questions.question: What are Java annotations?
questions.answer: Typed metadata attached to supported program elements for tools or runtime consumers to interpret.

questions.question: How do SOURCE, CLASS and RUNTIME retention differ?
questions.answer: SOURCE is discarded during compilation; CLASS is retained in class files; RUNTIME additionally makes metadata available through runtime reflection.

questions.question: What does annotation processing do?
questions.answer: It inspects source-level program models during compilation and can generate additional artifacts; it does not automatically execute annotated application behavior.

questions.question: Why can an annotation compile but do nothing?
questions.answer: Its required processor, runtime integration, registration or eligible invocation path may be absent.

questions.question: How would you design a custom annotation contract?
questions.answer: Define target, retention, supported consumers, defaults and failure behavior, then test both valid usage and unsupported targets or missing processing.

groups.title: Reflection and method handles
groups.mechanism: Reflection and method handles expose dynamic member access under access-control and module rules. Dynamic invocation does not erase type, security or packaging constraints.
groups.tradeOff: Flexibility can complicate AOT/native reachability and maintenance.
groups.verify: Test access across modules and actual packaged/native targets where supported.

questions.question: What is reflection used for?
questions.answer: Inspecting types and invoking or accessing supported members dynamically, common in tools and frameworks.

questions.question: When might a method handle be useful?
questions.answer: For a typed dynamic invocation mechanism integrated with JVM linkage facilities, while still requiring correct access and adaptation.

questions.question: How can strong module encapsulation affect reflection?
questions.answer: Non-open packages can restrict deep reflective access even when classpath-era code previously used it successfully.

questions.question: Why is setAccessible not a universal bypass?
questions.answer: Runtime access rules, module boundaries and platform restrictions can prevent the requested access.

questions.question: How would you reduce fragile reflection in a library?
questions.answer: Prefer public contracts or generated metadata, isolate unavoidable dynamic access and test supported module plus deployment configurations explicitly.

groups.title: Modules and packaging
groups.mechanism: JPMS describes module dependencies and exports; opens enables supported reflective access. Classpath and module-path behavior differ.
groups.tradeOff: Stronger encapsulation improves contracts while migration can reveal accidental dependency assumptions.
groups.verify: Run the artifact on its supported launch path with only declared dependencies.

questions.question: What does module-info.java describe?
questions.answer: A named module's dependencies, exported packages, services and reflective opening decisions.

questions.question: How do exports and opens differ?
questions.answer: Exports exposes package types for ordinary access; opens permits deeper runtime reflection under the module's rules.

questions.question: When is automatic-module behavior relevant?
questions.answer: When placing non-modular JARs on the module path; inspect derived names and compatibility rather than assuming full explicit modularity.

questions.question: Why can split packages complicate modularization?
questions.answer: Multiple modules containing the same package conflict with named-module organization and require dependency or package restructuring.

questions.question: How would you modularize a mature application?
questions.answer: Inventory actual dependencies and reflective use, isolate boundaries gradually and validate packaging plus runtime access before broad restructuring.

groups.title: Functional interfaces and lambdas
groups.mechanism: Lambdas implement target functional interfaces, capturing eligible lexical values. Capturing a reference does not freeze the object it points to.
groups.tradeOff: Concise callbacks can conceal retained objects and asynchronous ownership.
groups.verify: Modify captured mutable state concurrently and inspect lifetime plus exception behavior.

questions.question: What is a functional interface?
questions.answer: An interface with one abstract method contract suitable as a lambda target, accounting for inherited and Object-method rules.

questions.question: Why must captured local variables be effectively final?
questions.answer: The lambda captures their values under language rules, avoiding mutable local-variable capture semantics that would be ambiguous across lifetimes.

questions.question: How do Predicate, Function and Consumer differ?
questions.answer: Predicate tests, Function transforms and Consumer performs an action without returning a value; their types communicate different composition contracts.

questions.question: Why can a lambda retain an unexpectedly large object graph?
questions.answer: It can capture this or another long-lived reference, keeping the referenced graph reachable as long as the callback remains registered.

questions.question: How would you make asynchronous callbacks safe?
questions.answer: Define captured ownership, failure reporting, cancellation and deregistration; prefer immutable input values over uncontrolled shared mutable state.

groups.title: Concurrent collections
groups.mechanism: Concurrent containers provide specific operation guarantees, not whole-workflow atomicity. Snapshot, weakly consistent and copy-on-write iteration serve different workloads.
groups.tradeOff: Safer individual operations can still allow incorrect compound business decisions.
groups.verify: Race conflicting updates and verify invariants spanning all affected keys.

questions.question: When is CopyOnWriteArrayList useful?
questions.answer: For relatively small read-heavy collections with rare writes where snapshot iteration justifies copying on mutation.

questions.question: How does BlockingQueue support coordination?
questions.answer: It combines queue operations with waiting or timed admission/removal, allowing explicit producer-consumer capacity control.

questions.question: What does ConcurrentHashMap.compute protect?
questions.answer: The specified per-key computation under its contract; it does not make arbitrary external side effects or multi-key transitions atomic.

questions.question: Why can size followed by put exceed a concurrent limit?
questions.answer: Other threads can change the map between operations. Enforce capacity through a coordinated admission primitive or atomic state transition.

questions.question: How would you choose a concurrent container?
questions.answer: Start with operation semantics, iteration guarantees, contention and memory, then test the actual compound invariant rather than only thread-safe method calls.

groups.title: ThreadLocal and context
groups.mechanism: ThreadLocal associates values with threads, not business requests. Reused workers and asynchronous handoffs make explicit cleanup and propagation essential.
groups.tradeOff: Implicit context is convenient but can leak identities and retain memory.
groups.verify: Reuse workers across users and test exceptional completion plus handoff cleanup.

questions.question: What does ThreadLocal store?
questions.answer: A value associated with the current thread under that ThreadLocal key, rather than a globally shared value.

questions.question: When should a ThreadLocal value be removed?
questions.answer: At the defined ownership boundary, usually in finally for pooled-worker request context, to avoid retention or reuse by another request.

questions.question: Why does async execution not automatically preserve ThreadLocal state?
questions.answer: The task can run on another thread with different local values; use supported context capture and restoration rather than assuming transfer.

questions.question: How can pooled workers expose another request's identity?
questions.answer: A request can leave a value installed and the next task on that worker can observe it if cleanup is missing.

questions.question: How would you design context propagation safely?
questions.answer: Capture only approved immutable context, restore prior worker state after execution and keep security decisions tied to trusted explicit identities.

groups.title: Monitors and coordination
groups.mechanism: wait releases the owned monitor while waiting; notification only makes waiting threads eligible to compete again. Conditions require checking predicates in loops.
groups.tradeOff: Low-level coordination is powerful but easy to misuse; higher-level utilities often express intent better.
groups.verify: Control interleavings with barriers or latches and verify cancellation without sleep-based assumptions.

questions.question: How do wait and sleep differ?
questions.answer: wait requires monitor ownership and releases that monitor while waiting; sleep pauses the current thread without releasing held monitors.

questions.question: Why must wait be used inside a predicate loop?
questions.answer: Wakeups can be spurious or the condition can change before the thread reacquires the monitor.

questions.question: How does CountDownLatch differ from CyclicBarrier?
questions.answer: A latch typically represents one-way completion of a count; a barrier coordinates repeated rendezvous among participants under its contract.

questions.question: Why is notify not a guarantee the right task will proceed?
questions.answer: It selects a waiter without granting immediate execution or ensuring that waiter's predicate is true.

questions.question: How would you replace fragile wait-notify code?
questions.answer: State the condition and ownership model, then choose a queue, future, latch or explicit Condition that directly expresses the needed coordination.

groups.title: Reference types and reachability
groups.mechanism: Weak, soft and phantom references alter how reachability interacts with collection. They do not provide reliable business deadlines or external-resource cleanup.
groups.tradeOff: Reference-sensitive caches reduce explicit retention while making availability and timing less predictable.
groups.verify: Retain and release strong owners, then verify application correctness without requiring a particular collection time.

questions.question: What is a weak reference?
questions.answer: A reference that does not by itself keep its referent strongly reachable, allowing collection when other reachability conditions permit it.

questions.question: When is WeakHashMap useful?
questions.answer: For supported association lifetimes tied to weakly referenced keys, while ensuring values do not indirectly keep their own keys alive.

questions.question: Why are soft references not a precise cache-size policy?
questions.answer: Their reclamation depends on runtime memory behavior, so they cannot express a dependable maximum size or freshness contract.

questions.question: Why should finalization not own critical cleanup?
questions.answer: Its timing and execution are unreliable and it is deprecated for removal; release resources explicitly through clear ownership.

questions.question: How would you prevent a listener-related memory leak?
questions.answer: Keep registration handles, remove listeners at owner shutdown and inspect retaining paths rather than relying on weak references to conceal lifecycle errors.

groups.title: Serialization and trust boundaries
groups.mechanism: Serialization defines a wire or persistence contract, while deserialization consumes potentially hostile input. Type compatibility and security constraints remain explicit responsibilities.
groups.tradeOff: Generic object serialization is convenient but couples implementations and can expose dangerous object construction paths.
groups.verify: Test historical payloads, rejected types, size bounds and malformed data without using production secrets.

questions.question: How does Java serialization differ from a deliberate DTO protocol?
questions.answer: It encodes object-oriented state under serialization rules, often coupling consumers more closely to implementation types and evolution details.

questions.question: What does serialVersionUID control?
questions.answer: A serialization compatibility identifier used in class-version checks; matching it does not guarantee meaningful behavioral compatibility.

questions.question: Why is native Java deserialization of untrusted data risky?
questions.answer: It can construct complex object graphs and trigger dangerous type behavior; avoid it at untrusted boundaries and apply supported filters when unavoidable.

questions.question: Why does transient not mean data is securely erased?
questions.answer: It affects default serialization of a field, not all logging, custom serialization, memory retention or external copies.

questions.question: How would you evolve a persisted payload safely?
questions.answer: Use explicit schemas or DTO versions, tolerant readers, validated bounds and migration fixtures covering historical data plus rejected malicious forms.

groups.title: Networking and HTTP
groups.mechanism: Network calls involve DNS, connection establishment, pooling, TLS and response processing. Each stage can fail after different amounts of work or remote commitment.
groups.tradeOff: Connection reuse reduces cost while complicating deadlines and stale-connection handling.
groups.verify: Simulate connection failure, slow bodies, lost responses and cancellation after a side effect.

questions.question: What does Java HttpClient provide?
questions.answer: A standard HTTP client API with synchronous and asynchronous operations under configured protocol and transport capabilities.

questions.question: Why should an application reuse an HTTP client where appropriate?
questions.answer: Reuse can preserve connection pooling and configuration rather than creating new connection infrastructure for every request.

questions.question: How do TLS trust and hostname verification differ?
questions.answer: Trust validates the certificate chain under configured authorities; hostname verification checks that the certificate identifies the requested endpoint.

questions.question: Why can cancelling a request leave a remote write committed?
questions.answer: The remote server can finish before receiving cancellation or losing the connection; local completion state does not prove remote rollback.

questions.question: How would you bound network resource use?
questions.answer: Control connection and request limits, body sizes, acquisition waits and total deadlines, while defining unknown-outcome reconciliation.

groups.title: Files and filesystem safety
groups.mechanism: Path normalization, link resolution and authorization are separate concerns. Filesystem operations also have partial-failure and concurrent-update semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Simple path APIs do not automatically provide sandboxing or atomic multi-file updates.
groups.verify: Test traversal, symbolic links, interrupted writes and concurrent replacement in an isolated directory.

questions.question: How do Path and File differ conceptually?
questions.answer: Path participates in the NIO filesystem abstraction and richer operations, while File is an older pathname abstraction with different API ergonomics.

questions.question: When should a temporary file plus atomic move be considered?
questions.answer: For replacing a complete file without exposing partial content, while checking filesystem support, durability and cross-filesystem constraints.

questions.question: Why is normalize insufficient to prevent path traversal through symlinks?
questions.answer: It simplifies path syntax without resolving symbolic links or establishing the final authorized filesystem target.

questions.question: Why can checking file existence before writing still race?
questions.answer: Another process can change the target between the check and operation; use appropriate atomic creation and filesystem permissions.

questions.question: How would you design safe uploaded-file storage?
questions.answer: Use server-generated names, authorized directories, size limits and controlled link behavior, with atomic completion and cleanup of abandoned temporary files.

groups.title: Algorithms and complexity
groups.mechanism: Complexity estimates depend on input size and operation cost; database or network calls can dominate a superficially linear loop.
groups.tradeOff: Asymptotic improvements must be weighed against memory, locality and real workload sizes.
groups.verify: Compare against a simple reference on empty, duplicate, adversarial and large inputs.

questions.question: How do time and space complexity differ?
questions.answer: Time describes how work grows with input size; space describes additional storage growth under stated assumptions.

questions.question: When is a heap preferable to sorting every item?
questions.answer: When maintaining or retrieving a bounded top-k set or repeated extremes fits the operation pattern better than repeatedly ordering everything.

questions.question: Why can recursion overflow despite correct base cases?
questions.answer: A deep input can require more call-stack frames than available; choose iterative traversal or enforce depth bounds where necessary.

questions.question: Why can a hash-based linear algorithm still be vulnerable to poor inputs?
questions.answer: Collision behavior, allocation and memory can dominate; validate implementation guarantees and resource limits for untrusted cardinality.

questions.question: How would you review an algorithm embedded in a service?
questions.answer: Include data access, round trips, concurrency and payload bounds in the cost model, then verify both mathematical correctness and operational limits.

groups.title: JIT and runtime optimization
groups.mechanism: The JIT optimizes observed execution using runtime profiles, with deoptimization when assumptions change. Source appearance is not a reliable cost model.
groups.tradeOff: Optimizations can improve warm throughput while startup and polymorphic workloads behave differently.
groups.verify: Measure warm-up and steady state separately with a suitable benchmark and production-like inputs.

questions.question: What is JIT compilation?
questions.answer: Runtime compilation of executed bytecode into optimized machine code, guided by JVM implementation behavior and observed workload.

questions.question: Why separate startup from warmed performance?
questions.answer: Class loading, initialization and compilation work can dominate early requests while later execution benefits from optimized code.

questions.question: How can escape analysis affect allocation?
questions.answer: The runtime may prove some objects do not escape and optimize their representation or synchronization; it is not a universal source-level guarantee.

questions.question: Why can a microbenchmark report unrealistically fast code?
questions.answer: Unused results, constant inputs or insufficient warm-up can let optimization remove or transform the intended work.

questions.question: How would you compare two low-level optimizations?
questions.answer: Use controlled benchmarks with consumed results and representative distributions, then confirm end-to-end improvement and unchanged correctness.

groups.title: Design patterns in Java
groups.mechanism: Patterns name recurring design trade-offs rather than mandate class hierarchies. Select the smallest structure that expresses the actual variation or lifecycle.
groups.tradeOff: Abstraction helps stable variation points but speculative layers increase navigation and maintenance cost.
groups.verify: Add a second genuine behavior and evaluate whether the design changes locally and remains testable.

questions.question: When is Strategy appropriate?
questions.answer: When interchangeable algorithms share a stable contract and callers should select behavior without duplicating large conditional logic.

questions.question: How does Factory differ from Builder?
questions.answer: A factory selects or creates an object; a builder organizes staged construction and validation of a complex configuration or value.

questions.question: What does Decorator preserve?
questions.answer: The decorated interface while adding behavior around delegation, with explicit ordering and lifecycle responsibilities.

questions.question: Why can Singleton make testing and lifecycle harder?
questions.answer: Global shared state hides dependencies, retains resources and couples tests unless ownership and reset behavior are deliberately controlled.

questions.question: How would you justify introducing a design pattern?
questions.answer: Name the concrete variation or invariant, compare a simpler alternative and explain how the pattern improves change locality without obscuring behavior.

groups.title: Modern language boundaries
groups.mechanism: Java versions determine available language and API contracts. Preview features require explicit compilation/runtime agreement and can change before finalization.
groups.tradeOff: Modern syntax helps expression, but upgrades must preserve target-runtime compatibility.
groups.verify: Compile against the declared release and test both historical inputs and supported runtime launch modes.

questions.question: What does javac --release protect?
questions.answer: It checks language and supported platform API compatibility for the selected release; it does not make every external dependency compatible.

questions.question: When should a preview API be isolated?
questions.answer: When intentionally adopted under a pinned JDK, behind a boundary that makes later API changes and rollback manageable.

questions.question: How does switch expression exhaustiveness help?
questions.answer: It requires supported expression forms to produce a result or fail deliberately, reducing accidental fall-through and missing alternatives.

questions.question: Why is Java 21 structured concurrency not an ordinary stable API?
questions.answer: It is a preview API in that release and needs explicit preview flags plus matching runtime and build assumptions.

questions.question: How would you plan a Java runtime upgrade?
questions.answer: Inventory dependencies, removed behaviors and tooling, test container resources plus concurrency, and compare representative correctness and performance before rollout.

groups.title: Arrays and copying
groups.mechanism: Arrays have reified component types and fixed length. Copying an array normally copies element values, which can still be references to shared mutable objects.
groups.tradeOff: Compact indexed storage trades resizing flexibility for explicit bounds and ownership.
groups.verify: Test empty arrays, covariant writes and nested mutable elements after copying.

questions.question: How does an array differ from ArrayList?
questions.answer: An array has fixed length and a runtime component type; ArrayList is a resizable collection with generic compile-time element checking.

questions.question: When is System.arraycopy useful?
questions.answer: For supported bulk element copying, while preserving correct source/destination ranges and understanding that referenced objects are not deeply cloned.

questions.question: Why can assigning a String array to Object[] fail on a later write?
questions.answer: Array covariance permits the reference conversion, but storing a non-String object violates the array's runtime component type and throws ArrayStoreException.

questions.question: Why is cloning a two-dimensional array usually shallow?
questions.answer: It copies the outer array while the inner array references still point to the same nested arrays.

questions.question: How would you expose internal array data safely?
questions.answer: Return a copy or controlled read-only abstraction and define whether referenced mutable elements require additional defensive copying.

groups.title: Control flow and operators
groups.mechanism: Evaluation order, short-circuiting and numeric promotion determine observable behavior. Clear control flow is preferable to relying on subtle operator interactions.
groups.tradeOff: Concise expressions can hide side effects and exceptional paths.
groups.verify: Test false branches, null operands, overflow and boundary loop counts.

questions.question: How do && and & differ for boolean expressions?
questions.answer: Both can combine boolean values, but && short-circuits the right operand while & evaluates both operands.

questions.question: When should a switch expression be used?
questions.answer: When selecting a result among alternatives is clearer and supported by the target Java version, with explicit handling of all relevant cases.

questions.question: Why does left-to-right argument evaluation matter?
questions.answer: Side effects and exceptions in earlier arguments occur before later argument evaluation, so expressions are not freely interchangeable.

questions.question: How can a loop boundary produce an off-by-one failure?
questions.answer: Confusing inclusive and exclusive endpoints can skip the final element or access beyond the valid range, especially for empty input.

questions.question: How would you simplify complex branching safely?
questions.answer: State the input partitions and invariant, remove hidden side effects and verify each branch with boundary plus exceptional cases before refactoring.

groups.title: Interfaces and abstract types
groups.mechanism: Interfaces define supported behavior contracts, while abstract classes can share implementation and state. Default methods introduce inheritance rules without making every implementation change compatible.
groups.tradeOff: Shared behavior can reduce repetition but create diamond conflicts or unsupported assumptions.
groups.verify: Compile multiple-interface combinations and exercise existing implementations after API changes.

questions.question: How does an interface differ from an abstract class?
questions.answer: An interface primarily specifies a type contract with supported default/static behavior; an abstract class can define shared instance state and partial implementation.

questions.question: When should a default interface method be added?
questions.answer: When a meaningful compatible default exists and its interaction with existing implementations and inherited defaults has been reviewed.

questions.question: How are conflicting interface default methods resolved?
questions.answer: An implementing type may need an explicit override selecting or replacing behavior under Java's method-inheritance rules.

questions.question: Why can adding a method still break existing implementations?
questions.answer: Abstract additions can require implementation, while default additions can create conflicts or behavioral changes despite appearing source-compatible.

questions.question: How would you design an extension-friendly interface?
questions.answer: Keep responsibilities focused, define null/error/ordering contracts and evolve through explicit compatibility tests rather than exposing unstable implementation details.

groups.title: Regular expressions and parsing
groups.mechanism: Regular expressions match patterns under defined syntax and Unicode behavior. Some backtracking patterns can take excessive time on adversarial input.
groups.tradeOff: Compact matching is useful for bounded syntax, but structured parsers suit richer protocols.
groups.verify: Test near-matches, long repeated input and Unicode boundaries under explicit size limits.

questions.question: When is a regular expression appropriate?
questions.answer: For a bounded textual pattern that remains understandable and does not require a full structured-language parser.

questions.question: Why should a frequently reused Pattern be compiled once where appropriate?
questions.answer: It can avoid repeated compilation work while keeping Matcher instances and mutable matching state confined to each use.

questions.question: How do matches and find differ?
questions.answer: matches tests the entire input region against the pattern; find searches for a matching subsequence.

questions.question: Why can a regex become a denial-of-service risk?
questions.answer: Ambiguous nested repetition can cause catastrophic backtracking on crafted near-matching input, consuming excessive CPU.

questions.question: How would you validate a complex untrusted payload?
questions.answer: Bound its size, use a suitable parser and explicit schema, then reserve regex for narrow checks with adversarial performance tests.

groups.title: JDBC and database ownership
groups.mechanism: JDBC exposes connections, statements and result sets with explicit resource and transaction lifetimes. Pooling does not make connections safe for arbitrary concurrent sharing.
groups.tradeOff: Direct SQL gives control while requiring careful cleanup, binding and timeout policy.
groups.verify: Fail statement execution and commit independently, then verify rollback and resource return.

questions.question: What responsibilities does JDBC give application code?
questions.answer: Obtaining and releasing connections, executing parameterized SQL, consuming results and managing transaction behavior under the chosen integration.

questions.question: When should PreparedStatement be used?
questions.answer: For typed value binding and repeated statement execution without concatenating external values into SQL syntax.

questions.question: How does auto-commit affect JDBC operations?
questions.answer: When enabled, supported individual statements complete their own transaction behavior; multi-statement atomic work requires an intentional transaction boundary.

questions.question: Why can a connection leak cause timeouts with low database CPU?
questions.answer: The pool can run out of available connections even though the server is not busy executing queries.

questions.question: How would you handle an uncertain JDBC commit outcome?
questions.answer: Preserve operation identity and reconcile durable state; a lost connection during commit does not prove the transaction rolled back.

groups.title: Thread lifecycle and interruption
groups.mechanism: Thread states describe scheduling and waiting conditions rather than application progress. Interruption is a cooperative signal whose handling differs by operation.
groups.tradeOff: Low-level threads offer control but require explicit startup, publication and termination ownership.
groups.verify: Coordinate state transitions with latches and test interruption of waiting plus running tasks.

questions.question: What are Java's principal thread states?
questions.answer: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED, each describing a JVM thread lifecycle condition rather than a business status.

questions.question: How does start differ from calling run directly?
questions.answer: start requests execution on a new thread; calling run is an ordinary method call on the current thread.

questions.question: What does Thread.interrupted do to the interrupt flag?
questions.answer: It queries and clears the current thread's interrupt status, unlike isInterrupted which queries an instance without that clearing behavior.

questions.question: Why is interrupt not a guaranteed immediate stop?
questions.answer: Work must cooperate or use interruptible operations; CPU loops, libraries or remote effects may continue despite the signal.

questions.question: How would you terminate a worker robustly?
questions.answer: Stop admission, signal cancellation, unblock supported waits and await bounded termination while preserving recoverable ownership of unfinished work.

groups.title: ForkJoin and structured task ownership
groups.mechanism: ForkJoin supports divide-and-conquer scheduling, while structured concurrency associates child-task lifetime with a parent scope. Java 21 structured concurrency remains preview.
groups.tradeOff: Parallel composition can improve independent work but complicates blocking, cancellation and resource budgets.
groups.verify: Fail one branch and verify sibling cleanup plus bounded parent completion using the deployed JDK.

questions.question: When is ForkJoinPool useful?
questions.answer: For appropriately splittable computational tasks where work-stealing can balance independent subproblems with manageable overhead.

questions.question: Why can blocking I/O harm a shared ForkJoin workload?
questions.answer: Blocked workers can reduce available execution capacity or interfere with unrelated tasks using the same shared pool.

questions.question: What does structured concurrency try to make explicit?
questions.answer: The parent-child relationship of concurrent tasks, including joining, failure propagation and scope lifetime.

questions.question: Why can cancelling sibling tasks still leave a scope waiting?
questions.answer: Cancellation is cooperative; a child ignoring interruption or stuck in unresponsive I/O may not terminate promptly.

questions.question: How would you adopt Java 21 structured concurrency safely?
questions.answer: Pin the preview-enabled JDK, isolate the API and test failure, cancellation and close semantics, including children that do not cooperate.

groups.title: Cryptography and secure boundaries
groups.mechanism: Hashes, message authentication and encryption provide different properties. Correct algorithms still require key management, randomness and protocol-level validation.
groups.tradeOff: Security primitives are not interchangeable shortcuts for business trust or authorization.
groups.verify: Test tampering, wrong keys, expired credentials and safe failure without exposing secrets.

questions.question: How do hashing and encryption differ?
questions.answer: Hashing maps input to a digest without a general decryption operation; encryption protects recoverable plaintext using a key under a defined scheme.

questions.question: Why is an ordinary fast hash unsuitable for password storage?
questions.answer: Attackers can test guesses cheaply; use a vetted adaptive password-hashing scheme with unique salts and an appropriate work factor.

questions.question: When should SecureRandom be used?
questions.answer: For security-sensitive unpredictable values under a suitable provider, rather than ordinary pseudorandom utilities intended for simulation or convenience.

questions.question: Why does decoding a JWT not establish identity?
questions.answer: Decoding only parses data; trust requires signature verification plus issuer, audience, time and application authorization checks.

questions.question: How would you use Java cryptography safely?
questions.answer: Use vetted standard protocols and supported libraries, manage keys explicitly and test negative trust cases instead of inventing algorithms or logging sensitive material.

groups.title: Java toolchain and artifacts
groups.mechanism: Source compilation, bytecode compatibility and launch-time dependencies are separate stages. Reproducible builds require controlled toolchains and resolved artifacts.
groups.tradeOff: Packaging convenience does not eliminate dependency or runtime drift.
groups.verify: Build cleanly, inspect the produced artifact and launch with the declared runtime in isolation.

questions.question: How do JDK, runtime and bytecode relate?
questions.answer: The JDK supplies development tools and runtime components; Java source compiles to bytecode executed by a compatible runtime with required dependencies.

questions.question: What does a JAR contain?
questions.answer: An archive of classes and resources with optional metadata such as a manifest; executable behavior depends on its packaging and launch configuration.

questions.question: How do classpath and module path differ?
questions.answer: They provide different dependency organization and encapsulation models; named-module rules apply on the module path.

questions.question: Why can code compile but fail with NoSuchMethodError?
questions.answer: The runtime can load a binary-incompatible dependency version lacking the method signature against which the caller was compiled.

questions.question: How would you make a Java build reproducible?
questions.answer: Pin supported toolchains and dependency resolution, control generated inputs and verify the actual packaged artifact rather than relying on an IDE's retained outputs.

groups.title: Test design and executable contracts
groups.mechanism: Tests establish observable properties over selected cases, not universal correctness. Determinism and realistic fixtures are essential for useful regression evidence.
groups.tradeOff: Fast isolated tests and slower boundary tests serve different confidence needs.
groups.verify: Show that each regression fails with the defect present and passes with the intended behavior.

questions.question: How do unit and integration tests differ?
questions.answer: Unit tests isolate a focused decision or type; integration tests include the real interactions needed to verify a boundary contract.

questions.question: When are parameterized tests useful?
questions.answer: When one behavior needs systematic input partitions such as null, empty, duplicate, boundary and invalid values without copying test logic.

questions.question: What is property-based testing useful for?
questions.answer: Checking general invariants over many generated inputs, with meaningful generators and shrinking rather than replacing all domain-specific examples.

questions.question: Why are sleep-based concurrency tests fragile?
questions.answer: Scheduling varies across environments, so elapsed time does not prove the intended interleaving or completion happened.

questions.question: How would you test concurrent correctness deterministically?
questions.answer: Use barriers, latches or controlled executors to establish the target race and assert the business invariant plus resource cleanup.
